Resurgent and Emergent Diseases
Although great progress has been made in the treatment
and prevention of diseases in the last century, there is no
reason for complacence. Human health is constantly
threatened not only by emerging diseases but also by re-
emerging ones once thought to have been controlled or
eradicated. What causes new diseases? Why do the old
enemies resurge? What resources are available for us to
meet such challenges? What measures should we take
to prevent and reduce those threats? This unit helps you to
gain insight into those issues.

Summary1


• Old Enemies never die. (Para.1-4)

• Keeping our eyes on moving targets. (Para.5-12)

• Eternal vigilance or infernal results (Para.13-18)

Old Enemies never die.
• As the old saying goes, “Old enemies never
  die.” It is true with infectious diseases. Despite
  a string of impressive victories in medicine,
  conquest of microbes is an unfulfilled mission,
  and human beings are also confronted with
 new challenges posed by emerging diseases.
  AIDS and Ebola seemed to come from nowhere.
  Old afflictions such as diphtheria and Group A
  streptococcal infection have flared. It is evident
  that the battle against infectious diseases is far
  from won.

Keeping our eyes on moving targets.

•  The medical communities and public health authorities
  should not be misled by the complacent sentiment that the
  war against infectious disease has been won. Currently one
   inspiring observation is that joint efforts are being made for
   that purpose, with a new division established by WHO and
  fund provided by the Congress. Another mentionable
  endeavor is WHO's identification of six diseases whose
  worldwide re-emergence should be monitored: diphtheria,
   cholera, dengue fever, yellow fever, and bubonic plague. Such
  a list contributes to the realization that world health is
   indivisible. It is also important to realize that every returning
   condition is unique, each with a different wrinkle. TB is the
   result of socioeconomic conditions and human behavior;
  Group A strep may be due to a change in virulence and flu
   likewise changes its coat and in turn its level of virulence.

Eternal vigilance or infernal results.
• Eternal vigilance can keep future headlines free
  of news of worldwide pandemic. Vaccination
  cannot be emphasized more. Screening and
  diagnosis of infectious diseases should be
  carried out with stricter wide lines. Efforts
  should also be directed to the four areas of
  focus proposed by Bob Howard surveillance,
  science up-to-date and capable of dealing with
  what you discover in the field, appropriate
  prevention and control in place, and strong
  public health infrastructure in place.

    Writing a title

    •  Features of a good title
    •  Accuracy
     – Say what you mean, and mean what you say.
    • Conciseness
     – Write with precision and economy.
    •  Informative
